newsitem.title: UK: Better odds on EMU after stability pact - poll.
newsitem.headline: Better odds on EMU after stability pact - poll.

text.p: The odds of EMU going ahead on time have improved after agreement on a stability pact to enforce fiscal discipline, a Reuters survey of EMU experts showed on Wednesday.

The average of predictions on the percentage chance of European economic and monetary union (EMU) starting in 1999, from the December survey showed a rise of four points to 86 percent from 82 percent in November.

Thirty-two out of 36 contributors to the survey said the stability pact agreed at the recent Dublin summit of EU finance ministers and leaders overcame a major hurdle on the way to monetary union and meant EMU was still on track.

"The stability pact does make EMU more likely," said Jim Fralick, director of European equities at Morgan Stanley UK, noting that it may help sway German public opinion more in favour of a single currency.

"One of the big hang-ups was German public acceptance. I think they will be able to sell the pact to the German people." The stability pact will help reassure the inflation-phobic German public that the future single currency -- the euro -- would be as stable and credible as the mark, analysts said in the survey carried out between December 16 and 17.
Under the terms of the pact, any country which runs a budget deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product, as defined in the Maastricht Treaty, will face sanctions and fines.
Automatic exemptions will only apply where countries are forced to overspend by circumstances beyond their control or economic growth contracts by two percent or more in one year.

But even though the pact helps the process of EMU along there were still loopholes and analysts said there was too much political leeway to make the pact a completely credible way of ensuring fiscal discipline.

"The issue of how automatic it is was fudged and the GDP conditions are fuzzy in that politicians have to decide to impose the fine, which in practise they won't," said Gerry Holtham, director at the Institute for Public Policy Research.
"And there is no multi-national EU-wide statistical organisation to make independent judgements upon national statistics. Economic data will remain open to manipulation."
All 36 contributors to the survey expected Austria, Belguim, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands to form the core group of monetary union in 1999.
A majority, 34, of the experts expected Ireland and 28 expected Finland to join EMU in the first wave.
Contributor expectations for Spain and Portugal joining the core group in 1999 have been revised up slightly from the November survey.
Portugal's chances have improved by 18 points to 28 percent in December from 10 percent in November.
"The Portugese economy is in better shape than the Italian or Spanish economies," said Carls Hamilton, chief economist at Svenska Handelsbanken.
Forecasts made by the European Commission in early November show Portugal's budget deficit falling to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 from 4.0 percent in 1996.
More analysts now also believe that if EMU goes ahead, it will include Spain. In the December survey 28 percent expected Spain to be included from 17 percent from November.

Despite the Italian lira's re-entry to the European exchange rate mechanism in late November at a central parity rate of 990 lira to the mark, only 22 percent of analysts expect Italy to be accepted into monetary union in 1999.
